q0_0_1_3:
Definition

Inflammation is the local physiological response of vascularised living tissue to injury, designed to deliver leucocytes and plasma proteins to the site so that the offending agent can be destroyed and the damaged tissue repaired. Once the trigger is contained, the inflammatory reaction must resolve, organise, or progress — these are the three principal outcomes.

Possible Outcomes

  1. Resolution — complete restoration of normal architecture. Requires minimal parenchymal necrosis, intact basement membrane, rapid clearance of debris and a regenerative capacity of the local cells (labile/stable cells). Classic example: lobar pneumonia — macrophages clear the exudate and alveoli re-aerate.
  2. Healing by scarring (organisation / repair) — when tissue destruction is substantial or parenchyma cannot regenerate (permanent cells like neurons, cardiac myocytes), granulation tissue replaces the defect, matures into a collagenous scar. Example: myocardial infarction → fibrous scar.
  3. Abscess formation — when pyogenic bacteria are enclosed by fibrin and neutrophils, liquefactive necrosis produces pus enclosed in a pyogenic membrane. Common in S. aureus infections of skin, brain, lung.
  4. Chronic inflammation — persistence of the offending agent (intracellular microbes like M. tuberculosis, foreign bodies, autoimmunity) shifts the response to lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells with simultaneous tissue destruction and repair.
  5. Fibrosis — prolonged chronic inflammation drives TGF-β-mediated fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition, leading to organ dysfunction (e.g. lung fibrosis, cirrhosis).
  6. Spread — via lymphatics (lymphangitis, lymphadenitis), haematogenous (bacteraemia, septicaemia, pyaemia), or direct extension to adjacent structures (pleural empyema from pneumonia).
  7. Systemic effects — fever, leucocytosis, acute-phase response (CRP, ESR), and in severe cases septic shock with multi-organ dysfunction.
flowchart TD A[Acute Inflammation] --> B{Trigger cleared?} B -- Yes, minimal damage --> C[Resolution] B -- Yes, parenchyma destroyed --> D[Healing by Scarring] B -- No, pyogenic bacteria --> E[Abscess] B -- No, persistent agent --> F[Chronic Inflammation] F --> G[Fibrosis] A --> H[Lymphatic / Haematogenous Spread] A --> I[Systemic: Fever, Shock]

Clinical Pearl

Whether an inflammation resolves or scars depends chiefly on the regenerative capacity of the parenchymal cells (labile > stable > permanent) and the extent of basement membrane damage. A basally intact basement membrane permits complete regeneration; a destroyed one almost always heals with a scar.
q0_0_1_4:
Definition

Apoptosis (Kerr, Wyllie & Currie, 1972) is a form of programmed, energy-dependent, single-cell death characterised by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing and formation of apoptotic bodies — without significant inflammation. It corresponds to the "falling of leaves" in Greek.

Pathogenesis

Apoptosis is executed through two converging pathways that activate a cascade of caspases (cysteine-aspartate proteases):

  • Extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway — FasL/Fas (CD95), TNF/TNFR1, TRAIL/DR4-5 receptor engagement recruits FADD/TRADD → activation of initiator caspase-8 → caspase-3.
  • Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway — DNA damage, growth-factor withdrawal, hypoxia, radiation activate pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family members (Bax, Bak, Bid, Bad, PUMA, Noxa) which permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane → release of cytochrome-c into cytosol → Apaf-1 + cytochrome-c + procaspase-9 form the apoptosome → activates caspase-9 → caspase-3.

Both pathways converge on executioner caspase-3, which cleaves nuclear lamins, cytoskeleton, PARP-1 and ICAD (liberating DNase to fragment DNA into 180 bp multiples — "ladder pattern" on gel). Apoptotic bodies are then phagocytosed by neighbouring cells or macrophages through phosphatidylserine (flipped to outer leaflet), thrombospondin and vitronectin receptors — without an inflammatory response.

Regulation: anti-apoptotic Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1 oppose Bax/Bak. p53 induces apoptosis in damaged cells by upregulating Bax, PUMA, Noxa.

flowchart TD A[Death receptor ligand] --> B[Fas/TNFR] B --> C[Caspase-8] C --> D[Caspase-3] E[Stress: DNA damage, hypoxia, ROS] --> F[p53 / Bax, Bak] F --> G[Mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation] G --> H[Cytochrome-c + Apaf-1] H --> I[Apoptosome → Caspase-9] I --> D D --> J[Chromatin condensation, DNA ladder, apoptotic bodies]

Two Differences — Necrosis vs Apoptosis

FeatureNecrosisApoptosis
Cell sizeEnlarged (swelling, oncosis)Shrunken
InflammationAlways presentAbsent
DNA breakdownRandom, diffuse (smear)Internucleosomal 180-bp ladder
ATP requirementNone (passive)Active, ATP-dependent

Clinical Pearl

Apoptosis is physiologically silent; necrosis is always noisy. Excessive apoptosis causes neurodegeneration (Alzheimer, Parkinson) and aplastic anaemia; deficient apoptosis drives autoimmunity (SLE) and cancer (follicular B-cell lymphoma due to Bcl-2 over-expression from t(14;18)).
q0_0_1_5:
Definition

Amyloidosis refers to a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by extracellular deposition of insoluble, fibrillar β-pleated sheet proteinaceous material — amyloid — in various tissues.

Pathogenesis

Amyloid fibrils are 7.5–10 nm rigid, non-branching filaments. All amyloid share a common β-pleated sheet conformation confirmed by Congo-red apple-green birefringence under polarised light and a characteristic cross-β X-ray diffraction pattern. A glycoprotein called serum amyloid P (SAP) and glycosaminoglycans are universally associated and stabilise the fibrils, preventing their breakdown.

Fibrillogenesis involves: (1) overproduction of a precursor protein; (2) misfolding into β-sheets; (3) proteolytic cleavage where needed; (4) aggregation and tissue deposition. The most important precursors are:

  • AL (amyloid light chain) — monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains from plasma-cell dyscrasias (multiple myeloma, B-cell lymphoma, MGUS).
  • AA (amyloid-associated) — derived from serum amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase reactant; chronic inflammation (TB, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, bronchiectasis, leprosy).
  • ATTR (transthyretin) — familial (mutant TTR) and wild-type / senile systemic amyloidosis (cardiac).
  • Aβ2-microglobulin — dialysis-associated.
  • Aβ peptide — Alzheimer disease (cerebral, vascular).
  • Localised — endocrine (medullary thyroid CA — calcitonin), atrial amyloid (ANP), type-2 diabetes islet amyloid (amylin / IAPP).

Classification

TypePrecursorClinical Setting
Systemic AL (primary)Ig light chainMultiple myeloma, MGUS, B-cell lymphoma
Systemic AA (secondary)Serum amyloid AChronic inflammation: TB, RA, IBD, bronchiectasis, leprosy, osteomyelitis
Hereditary/familialMutant transthyretin, fibrinogen Aα, apolipoprotein A-I, lysozymeFamilial amyloid polyneuropathy, nephropathy
Dialysis-relatedβ2-microglobulinLong-term haemodialysis; carpal tunnel, arthropathy
Senile systemicWild-type TTRCardiac amyloidosis in elderly
Cerebral / ageingAβ peptideAlzheimer disease
Endocrine / localisedCalcitonin, amylin (IAPP), ANP, prolactinMedullary thyroid CA, type-2 diabetes, atrial amyloid

Diagnosis

  1. Tissue biopsy — abdominal subcutaneous fat pad aspiration is the gold standard for systemic amyloidosis (sensitivity ~80%, specificity 100%). Rectal, gingival, renal or bone-marrow biopsies are alternatives.
  2. Congo red stain — orange-pink under light, apple-green birefringence under polarised light; pathognomonic.
  3. Crystal violet — metachromatic rose-pink.
  4. Thioflavin T — yellow-green fluorescence under UV.
  5. Immunohistochemistry / immunofluorescence — anti-κ, λ, SAA, TTR antibodies classify the type.
  6. Electron microscopy — non-branching 7.5–10 nm rigid fibrils.
  7. Mass spectrometry (Laser Microdissection / Mass Spectrometry, LMD/MS) — modern gold standard for typing.
  8. SAP scintigraphy — images systemic amyloid load.
  9. Supportive workup — serum/urine electrophoresis & free light-chain assay (AL), ESR/CRP & SAA (AA), echocardiography & cardiac MRI (cardiac amyloid), TTR gene sequencing.

Clinical Pearl

Macroglossia + periorbital purpura + nephrotic-range proteinuria + restrictive cardiomyopathy = think AL amyloidosis. Always send serum free light chain ratio and urine for Bence-Jones protein. Fat-pad aspiration combined with Congo red gives the quickest diagnosis.

Definition

Thromboembolism is the dislodgement of a thrombus (or part of it) from its site of formation and its impaction in a downstream vessel. The dislodged fragment is an embolus. >99% of emboli are thromboembolic.

Pathogenesis

Thrombus formation is governed by Virchow's triad:

  1. Endothelial injury — exposes subendothelial collagen & tissue factor, disrupts antithrombotic properties of endothelium (dominant in cardiac and arterial thrombi).
  2. Abnormal blood flow — stasis (DVT, atrial fibrillation) and turbulence (aneurysms, bifurcations) prevent dilution of clotting factors and bring platelets into contact with endothelium.
  3. Hypercoagulability — primary (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin/protein C/S deficiency) and secondary (malignancy, pregnancy, OCPs, immobilisation, surgery, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome).

Once formed, a thrombus may: (i) lyse, (ii) organise into a scar, (iii) recanalise, or (iv) embolise. Emboli fragment most readily when loosely attached to a vein wall or to a roughened aortic/atrial surface. DVT of the deep calf, popliteal, femoral or iliac veins is the source of pulmonary embolism; left atrial thrombi (in mitral stenosis / AF) and left ventricular mural thrombi (post-MI) embolise to the systemic circulation — brain, spleen, kidney, gut, limbs.

flowchart TD A[Virchow Triad: Injury, Stasis, Hypercoagulability] --> B[Thrombus formation] B --> C[Dislodgement] C --> D{Origin} D -- Venous --> E[Pulmonary embolism] D -- Left heart / arterial --> F[Systemic embolism: brain, spleen, kidney, gut, limbs] D -- Right heart --> E B --> G[Recanalisation / Organisation]

Types of Thromboembolism

  • Pulmonary thromboembolism — saddle PE (large), lobar, micro-embolic; 95% arise from DVT of lower limbs.
  • Systemic arterial embolism — mural thrombus (post-MI), atrial thrombus (AF, mitral stenosis), vegetations (endocarditis), aortic aneurysm.
  • Paradoxical embolism — venous thrombus crosses a patent foramen ovale or ASD to reach systemic circulation.
  • Septic embolism — infected thrombus → pyaemic abscesses (e.g. IE, Lemierre syndrome).
  • Fat embolism — long-bone fractures, liposuction; triad of respiratory distress, neurological symptoms, petechial rash at 24–72 h.
  • Amniotic fluid embolism — during labour; sudden dyspnoea, hypotension, DIC.
  • Air embolism — >100 mL needed; chest trauma, neurosurgery, decompression sickness ("caisson disease").

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • DVT — D-dimer (high NPV), compression ultrasonography (gold standard), venography (historical).
  • Pulmonary embolism — Wells score → D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiography (gold standard, filling defect), V/Q scan (if CTPA contraindicated), echocardiography (right heart strain — McConnell's sign), troponin/BNP.
  • Hypercoagulability workup — PT, aPTT, platelet count, fibrinogen, D-dimer, antithrombin, protein C & S, Factor V Leiden (APC resistance), prothrombin G20210A, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin & anti-β2-GPI antibodies, homocysteine.
  • Arterial embolism — ECG (AF, MI), echocardiography (vegetations, mural thrombus, atrial thrombus), CT angiography, carotid Doppler.

Clinical Pearl

Sudden dyspnoea + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia in a post-operative or bedridden patient = pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise. A normal D-dimer excludes PE in low-risk patients (Wells ≤4); confirm with CT pulmonary angiography. Anticoagulate early — heparin bridge to warfarin/DOAC.

Definition

Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN) — also called erythroblastosis fetalis — is a condition in which transplacental passage of maternal IgG antibodies against fetal red-cell antigens causes immune-mediated haemolysis of fetal erythrocytes, leading to fetal anaemia, jaundice and, in severe cases, hydrops fetalis or kernicterus.

Pathogenesis

Maternal IgG (the only immunoglobulin that crosses placenta) is raised against fetal RBC antigens inherited from the father but absent in the mother. Sensitisation occurs in a previous pregnancy, miscarriage, abortion or transfusion. Subsequent pregnancies with an antigen-positive fetus trigger an anamnestic IgG response; antibodies cross placenta, bind fetal RBCs and cause extravascular haemolysis via Fc-receptor macrophages in the fetal spleen and liver.

TypeAntibodySeverity
Rh (D) incompatibilityAnti-D IgGCommonest severe; usually 2nd+ pregnancy
ABO incompatibilityAnti-A / Anti-B (IgG)Mild; first pregnancy possible; group O mother + A/B infant
Minor antigensAnti-c, Anti-E, Anti-Kell, Anti-Duffy, Anti-KiddVariable; Kell causes severe anaemia by erythroid suppression

Laboratory Evaluation

  1. Antenatal — maternal
    • Blood group & Rh typing (every mother at booking).
    • Indirect antiglobulin / indirect Coombs test — screens maternal serum for IgG antibodies at 12, 28 weeks.
    • Anti-D titre — >1:16 is significant; serial doubling titres warrant fetal monitoring.
    • Cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) in maternal plasma — RhD genotype of fetus (non-invasive).
  2. Antenatal — fetal
    • Middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity Doppler — >1.5 MoM predicts moderate/severe anaemia.
    • Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS) — direct fetal Hb, bilirubin, blood group, Coombs.
    • Amniocentesis — delta-OD450 of amniotic fluid (Liley chart, Queenan curve).
    • Serial ultrasound — hydrops (ascites, pleural effusion, skin oedema, polyhydramnios).
  3. Postnatal — neonatal
    • Cord blood: blood group, direct antiglobulin test (DAT / direct Coombs), Hb, bilirubin, reticulocyte count, peripheral smear (spherocytes, nucleated RBCs).
    • Serial serum bilirubin (every 4–6 h) — "rate of rise" drives phototherapy/exchange decision.
    • Kernicterus watch — lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia, high-pitched cry, seizures.

Safety Precautions

  • Antenatal anti-D prophylaxis — Rh-negative mother receives 300 µg (1500 IU) anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks, within 72 h of delivery, and after any sensitising event (abortion, APH, ectopic, trauma, amniocentesis, external cephalic version).
  • Confirm fetomaternal haemorrhage (FMH) by Kleihauer-Betke test or flow cytometry; give extra anti-D if large FMH.
  • Avoid unnecessary instrumentation and traumatic deliveries.
  • Handle fetal blood samples with universal precautions — risk of needle-stick, infection, bleeding.
  • Phototherapy — protect eyes with eye-pads, monitor temperature and hydration.
  • Exchange transfusion — use irradiated, CMV-negative, leucocyte-reduced, antigen-negative (O-negative or ABO/Rh-compatible) blood; aseptic technique; monitor Ca2+, glucose, pH, platelets.
  • Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) reduces exchange rate in severe HDN.
  • Breast-feeding is not contraindicated in ABO/Rh HDN — milk jaundice and breastfeeding jaundice are different entities.

Clinical Pearl

Anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks + within 72 h of delivery has reduced Rh-haemolytic disease of the newborn by >95%. The first pregnancy is usually the sensitising event — hence the rationale for routine antenatal prophylaxis even in primigravida.
q0_0_1_0:
Overview

Urinalysis is one of the oldest, cheapest, and most informative bedside investigations — a "liquid biopsy" of the kidney & urinary tract. A complete examination has three components: Physical, Chemical, and Microscopic.

1. Physical Examination

ParameterNormalAbnormal — Clinical Significance
Volume600–2000 mL/day↑ Polyuria (DM, DI, CKD); ↓ Oliguria (<400 mL/day), Anuria (<100 mL/day)
ColourPale yellow / amber (urochrome)Red — haematuria, beeturia, porphyria, rifampicin; Brown — old blood, bilirubin; Smoky — glomerulonephritis; Milky — chyluria, pyuria
Appearance / TurbidityClearCloudy — phosphates (alkaline), urates (acid), pyuria, chyluria; Frothy — proteinuria
OdourAromaticPungent — ammonia (UTI); Fruity — ketones (DKA); Mousy — phenylketonuria; Maple syrup — maple syrup urine disease
Specific gravity1.003–1.030↑ Dehydration, glycosuria, contrast; ↓ DI, over-hydration; Fixed 1.010 — chronic renal disease (isosthenuria)
pH4.5–8.0 (avg ~6, acidic)↑ Alkaline — UTI with urea-splitting organisms (Proteus), RTA type 1, vomiting; ↓ Acidic — DKA, lactic acidosis, fever, diarrhoea

2. Chemical Examination

Modern dipsticks (e.g. Combur, Multistix) use dry chemistry pads read visually or by automated reader.

  • pH — double indicator (methyl red / bromothymol blue).
  • Specific gravity — ionic strength indicator (bromothymol blue).
  • Protein — tetrabromophenol blue dye-binding; detects mainly albumin (false negative for Bence-Jones proteins → use sulphosalicylic acid test / protein electrophoresis).
  • Glucose — glucose oxidase-peroxidase (GOD-POD); specific for glucose only. False + with peroxide cleaners; false − with high dose vitamin C.
  • Ketones — sodium nitroprusside reaction with acetoacetate (not β-hydroxybutyrate).
  • Blood / Haemoglobin — peroxidase-like activity of Hb / myoglobin lyses chromogen; intact RBCs produce speckled pattern; lysed RBCs / myoglobin produce uniform colour.
  • Bilirubin — diazo reaction (2,4-dichloroaniline); absent in normal urine.
  • Urobilinogen — Ehrlich aldehyde reaction; normally present in traces; absent in complete biliary obstruction; raised in haemolysis & hepatocellular dysfunction.
  • Nitrite — Greiss reaction; positive with nitrate-reducing bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) — needs urine to dwell ≥4 h in bladder; first morning sample most useful.
  • Leucocyte esterase — detects esterases from lysed WBCs; sensitive for pyuria.

3. Microscopic Examination

Performed on freshly voided, midstream, centrifuged urine (10 mL at 1500 rpm × 5 min), examined under low & high power. Findings are reported per high-power field (HPF).

Cells

  • RBCs — >3 RBC/HPF = haematuria. Dysmorphic RBCs & RBC casts → glomerular bleeding; Isomorphic RBCs → urological cause (stones, tumour, infection).
  • WBCs — >5 WBC/HPF = pyuria. Sterile pyuria — TB, Chlamydia, gonococcus, stones, interstitial nephritis, partially treated UTI.
  • Epithelial cells — squamous (contamination); transitional (catheterised, catheter-induced); renal tubular (ATN, acute interstitial nephritis, acute tubular injury).
  • Oval fat bodies — lipid-laden renal tubular cells; "Maltese cross" appearance under polarised light — nephrotic syndrome.

Casts (formed in distal & collecting tubules; matrix = Tamm-Horsfall protein)

  • Hyaline — clear, colourless; normal after exercise, dehydration; nonspecific.
  • Granular — degenerated tubular cells; "muddy brown" coarse granular casts → acute tubular necrosis.
  • RBC casts — pathognomonic of glomerulonephritis (e.g. post-streptococcal, IgA nephropathy).
  • WBC casts — acute pyelonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis.
  • Broad waxy casts — formed in dilated tubules of chronically diseased kidney; chronic renal failure.
  • Fatty casts — nephrotic syndrome.

Crystals

  • Calcium oxalate (envelope / "envelope" appearance) — acidic urine; ethylene glycol poisoning shows envelope & needle forms.
  • Uric acid (rhomboid / "whetstone") — acidic urine; gout, tumour lysis.
  • Triple phosphate ("coffin-lid") — alkaline urine; Proteus UTI (struvite stones).
  • Cystine (hexagonal, benzene ring) — cystinuria.
  • Sulphonamide, radiographic contrast — drug-induced crystals with acute kidney injury.

Organisms

  • Bacteria (rods / cocci) — UTI; confirm with culture & sensitivity.
  • Trichomonas vaginalis, yeast (Candida), Schistosoma haematobium ova — depending on geography.
flowchart LR A[Fresh MSU sample] --> B[Physical - colour / clarity / SG / pH] A --> C[Chemical - dipstick 10 parameters] A --> D[Centrifuge 5 min 1500 rpm] D --> E[Sediment microscopy - cells / casts / crystals / organisms] B & C & E --> F[Correlate with clinical picture] F --> G[Diagnosis]

Clinical Pearl

The combination "dipstick protein + dysmorphic RBCs + RBC casts" is the bedside fingerprint of glomerular disease and warrants urgent nephrology referral & renal biopsy. Conversely, dipstick blood with isomorphic RBCs and no proteinuria points to a urological cause — investigate with imaging/cystoscopy, not biopsy.

Overview

Neutrophils are the first responders of acute inflammation. Their journey from the bloodstream into the tissue is described by a 5-step paradigm — each step governed by specific adhesion molecules and chemokines. Failure of any step produces immunodeficiency (e.g. leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 due to CD18 deficiency → recurrent infections without pus).

flowchart TD A[Margination] --> B[Rolling] B --> C[Adhesion / Firm arrest] C --> D[Transmigration / Diapedesis] D --> E[Chemotaxis] E --> F[Phagocytosis at site]

Step 1 — Margination

  • In normal laminar flow, RBCs occupy the axial (central) stream and WBCs are pushed to the periphery — the "plasma skimming" effect.
  • With inflammation, vasodilation slows blood flow & increases viscosity → neutrophils settle against the endothelium (margination).

Step 2 — Rolling (Loose, Transient Adhesion)

  • Selectin family mediates weak, reversible binding — bond breaks & re-forms, so leucocytes "roll" along the endothelium.
  • E-selectin (endothelium; induced by TNF-α & IL-1 within 2 hours).
  • P-selectin (preformed in Weibel-Palade bodies; mobilised to surface within minutes by histamine & thrombin).
  • L-selectin (on neutrophil surface).
  • Ligands — sialyl-Lewis X on leucocytes; PSGL-1 (P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1).

Step 3 — Adhesion / Firm Arrest

  • Chemokines (IL-8, C5a, LTB4) activate neutrophils and trigger conformational change in integrins on the leucocyte surface → high-affinity binding.
  • β2 integrins (CD18) — LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18), Mac-1 (CD11b/CD18) on the neutrophil.
  • Ligands on endothelium — ICAM-1 (inducible by TNF-α, IL-1) and ICAM-2.
  • This step is the tightest — once integrins bind ICAM-1, the neutrophil stops rolling and flattens.

Step 4 — Transmigration / Diapedesis

  • Neutrophils crawl to intercellular junctions and squeeze between endothelial cells.
  • Mediated by PECAM-1 (CD31) — homophilic binding between endothelial & leucocyte CD31.
  • Other molecules — VE-cadherin, CD99, JAM (junctional adhesion molecules).
  • The neutrophil then crosses the basement membrane by secreting collagenases (MMP-8, MMP-9) & elastase.

Step 5 — Chemotaxis

  • Directed migration along a chemical gradient toward the site of injury.
  • Exogenous chemotaxins — bacterial products (N-formyl peptides like fMet-Leu-Phe).
  • Endogenous chemotaxins — C5a, LTB4, IL-8, fibrinopeptides, platelet-activating factor (PAF).
  • Receptors — G-protein coupled receptors; ligand binding triggers actin polymerisation at the leading edge (pseudopod formation).

Step 6 — Phagocytosis (after arrival)

  • Recognition & attachment — enhanced by opsonins (IgG, C3b); binds FcγR & CR1/CR3.
  • Engulfment — pseudopods encircle the particle → phagosome → phagolysosome.
  • Killing — two mechanisms:
    • Oxygen-dependent — NADPH oxidase (respiratory burst) → superoxide → H₂O₂ → via MPO + Cl⁻ → hypochlorous acid (bleach). Defect = chronic granulomatous disease.
    • Oxygen-independent — lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins, proteases, low pH.

Clinical Correlations — When the Cascade Fails

  • LAD-1 — CD18 deficiency; neutrophils can't bind ICAM-1 → no pus formation despite high neutrophil count; delayed umbilical stump separation.
  • LAD-2 — fucose transporter defect (Sialyl-Lewis X absent) → mentally retarded child with recurrent infections.
  • Chronic Granulomatous Disease — NADPH oxidase defect → recurrent catalase-positive infections (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia); diagnostic NBT/DHR test.
  • Chédiak-Higashi syndrome — giant lysosomal granules; defective chemotaxis & degranulation; partial albinism.
  • Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome — impaired chemotaxis → cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, eczema, high IgE.

Clinical Pearl

Glucocorticoids reduce ICAM-1 expression on endothelium — explaining both their anti-inflammatory benefit and their propensity to impair bacterial clearance. This is also why a patient on steroids may show a paucity of pus at an infection site even with florid sepsis — clinical signs are masked, and a high index of suspicion is required.

Overview

Chemical mediators of inflammation are released from cells (mast cells, platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, endothelium) and from plasma (kinin, complement, coagulation/fibrinolytic systems). Here we focus on the cell-derived mediators — the viva expects you to list, classify, and indicate actions.

Cell-Derived Mediators — Master List

MediatorSourceMajor Actions
HistamineMast cells, basophils, platelets (preformed in granules)Vasodilation (H1 on vascular smooth muscle); ↑ vascular permeability (endothelial contraction); bronchoconstriction; itching (H1 on sensory nerves); gastric acid secretion (H2)
Serotonin (5-HT)Platelets, mast cells (rodent)Vasodilation & ↑ permeability (less potent than histamine)
Prostaglandins (PGs)All nucleated cells (COX-1 constitutive, COX-2 inducible from arachidonic acid)PGE2 — vasodilation, fever, potentiate pain (with bradykinin), ↑ permeability (with histamine). PGD2 — mast-cell vasodilation. PGI2 (prostacyclin) — vasodilation & platelet inhibition. TXA2 — vasoconstriction & platelet aggregation (from platelets).
Leukotrienes (LTs)Leucocytes (5-lipoxygenase pathway)LTB4 — potent chemotaxin & neutrophil activator. LTC4, LTD4, LTE4 (slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis) — bronchoconstriction 100–1000× histamine; ↑ vascular permeability
Lipoxins (LXs)Platelets (from neutrophil-derived LTA4)Anti-inflammatory — inhibit neutrophil recruitment; promote resolution. "Brake" of inflammation
Platelet-Activating Factor (PAF)Mast cells, neutrophils, monocytes, endothelium, plateletsPlatelet aggregation & degranulation; vasodilation; ↑ permeability (1000–10 000× histamine); chemotaxis; bronchoconstriction
Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS)Neutrophils, macrophages (NADPH oxidase)Killing of microbes (O₂⁻, H₂O₂, HOCl); tissue damage (lipid peroxidation, protease activation); inactivate antiproteases
NO (Nitric Oxide)Endothelium (eNOS), macrophages (iNOS), neurons (nNOS)Vasodilation (smooth-muscle relaxation via cGMP); antiplatelet; antimicrobial (reactive nitrogen species); cytotoxicity in chronic inflammation
CytokinesMacrophages, lymphocytes, endothelium, mast cellsTNF-α, IL-1 — endothelial activation, fever, acute-phase response, cachexia. IL-6 — acute-phase synthesis in liver. IL-8 (CXCL8) — neutrophil chemotaxis. IL-12 — Th1 polarisation. IFN-γ — macrophage activation
ChemokinesAll nucleated cellsChemotaxis of leucocytes to site of injury; classified CC, CXC, C, CX3C
Lysosomal enzymesNeutrophils (azurophilic & specific granules), macrophagesProteases (elastase, collagenase, cathepsin) → tissue destruction; lysozyme → bacterial wall lysis; lactoferrin → iron chelation; myeloperoxidase → microbial killing (with H₂O₂ + Cl⁻)
DefensinsNeutrophils, intestinal Paneth cells, epitheliaArginine-rich cationic peptides → punch holes in bacterial membranes
NeuropeptidesSensory nerve endings (C fibres)Substance P — vasodilation, ↑ permeability, pain transmission; CGRP — vasodilation
flowchart TD A[Cell membrane phospholipid] -->|Phospholipase A2| B[Arachidonic Acid] B -->|Cyclooxygenase COX-1 / COX-2| C[Prostaglandins
PGE2 / PGI2 / TXA2 / PGD2] B -->|5-Lipoxygenase| D[Leukotrienes
LTB4 / LTC4 / LTD4 / LTE4] B -->|Lipooxygenase interaction| E[Lipoxins
anti-inflammatory] C --> F[Vasodilation, fever, pain, platelet modulation] D --> G[Chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction, permeability] E --> H[Resolution of inflammation]

Functional Summary (for viva recall)

  • Vasodilation — histamine, PGE2, PGI2, NO, PAF.
  • ↑ Vascular Permeability — histamine, bradykinin (plasma), PAF, LTC4/D4/E4, substance P.
  • Pain — bradykinin, PGE2 (sensitises nociceptors), substance P.
  • Fever — PGE2 (acts on hypothalamus), IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6 (acute-phase pyrogens).
  • Chemotaxis — LTB4, C5a, IL-8, bacterial f-Met peptides, PAF.
  • Tissue damage — ROS, lysosomal proteases (elastase, collagenase), NO.

Clinical Pearl — Drug Targets

  • NSAIDs block COX-1 & COX-2 → ↓ PGs & thromboxanes. COX-2 selective (celecoxib) spares gastric protection (PGE2) but ↑ thrombotic risk (loss of PGI2 leaving TXA2 unopposed).
  • Corticosteroids induce lipocortin-1 → ↓ phospholipase A2 → ↓ both PGs & LTs. Comprehensive anti-inflammatory action.
  • Leukotriene-receptor antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast) block LTD4 receptor — useful in asthma, especially aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
  • Anti-IgE (omalizumab) & anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab) target upstream signalling in severe asthma.
  • Anti-TNF biologics (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept) — TNF-α blockade in rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis.
